title: Dracula is back from the dead
gist: Hammer Films, now owned by theatre impresario John Gore, has completed a 4K restoration of its 1958 Dracula that restores three minutes of censored footage found in the Warner Bros archives. The revived studio is pairing back-catalogue restoration with new productions, and Gore bought Silver Salt Restoration to vertically integrate the restoration work.

insights.claim: Hammer Films, now owned by theatre impresario John Gore, is back in business both making new movies and restoring its classic back catalogue to 21st-century standards.
insights.speaker: David Barnett
insights.so_what: Illustrates a back-catalogue monetisation strategy for legacy film IP.

insights.claim: After buying Hammer, John Gore also bought Silver Salt Restoration, reasoning that if he was spending money restoring a large back catalogue he might as well own the restoration company.
insights.speaker: David Barnett
insights.so_what: An example of vertical integration in film-library exploitation, capturing restoration margins in-house.

insights.claim: Hammer's first original film under the new ownership, Ithaqua, draws on indigenous Canadian mythology, stars Luke Hemsworth and is currently on the film festival circuit.
insights.speaker: David Barnett
insights.so_what: Shows the studio is investing in new IP alongside its library.

insights.claim: Hammer completed a 4K restoration of its 1958 Dracula this year, adding back three minutes of footage cut by the British Board of Film Censors that was thought lost forever.
insights.speaker: David Barnett
insights.so_what: Restored, uncut versions create a premium re-release product from existing IP.

insights.claim: The uncut footage was found by George Feltenstein in the Warner Bros archives in Los Angeles, after Hammer's search for the only known uncut release print, in Japan, drew a blank; Warner Bros holds the US rights to the film.
insights.speaker: David Barnett
insights.so_what: Highlights the value locked in studio archives and rights-holder cooperation.

insights.claim: The restored Dracula is on a 144-theatre cinematic release tour followed by a DVD/Blu-ray release in November.
insights.speaker: David Barnett
insights.so_what: Shows a multi-window release strategy (theatrical event plus physical media) for restored classics.
insights.quote: Dracula is on a 144-theatre cinematic release tour

insights.claim: There have been around a hundred cinematic outings for Dracula since Bram Stoker's 1897 novel, and Hammer made nine Dracula films, with Christopher Lee starring in seven.
insights.speaker: David Barnett
insights.so_what: Dracula is a perennially monetisable public-domain character.

insights.claim: Barnett argues Hammer's distinctive contribution, compared with Universal's Bela Lugosi version, was introducing sex, sensuality and gore into the vampire legend.
insights.speaker: David Barnett
insights.so_what: Brand differentiation through tone kept Hammer's catalogue culturally relevant.

insights.claim: Despite taking major liberties with Stoker's novel to fit an 82-minute film, Hammer's 1958 Dracula became one of the defining cinematic adaptations.
insights.speaker: David Barnett
insights.so_what: Fidelity to source matters less than distinctive execution for lasting IP value.
